title: Meet the Superhero Midwives Saving Lives in Colombia's Jungles
summary: What if you were about to have a baby, but the nearest hospital was days away? In parts of Colombia, thick jungles and rivers make it almost impossible to reach a doctor. That's where superheroes like Nohemí Manco step in. She's a traditional midwife—a person trained to help moms give birth. Manco was only 14 when she delivered her first baby: her sister's! She wasn't scared because she'd watched her mom do it many times. Now 53, she's helped bring about 1,200 babies into the world. "When a baby starts coming, it feels like sunrise," she says. "Everything is dark, and then it's dawn." In Colombia, these midwives are called "parteras tradicionales." They are often the only healthcare for pregnant women in faraway villages. But many midwives say doctors and nurses have been mean to them. They've been laughed at or turned away from hospitals. "We felt the tradition was being lost because there was so much discrimination," says midwife Yuvianis Florez, 36. Still, the midwives don't hate modern medicine. They want to work together with doctors to keep moms and babies safe. A recent survey found over 1,700 traditional midwives in the region. But almost half are over 60, and many can't read. Manco hopes young people will learn the skills so this lifesaving tradition doesn't disappear.
why_it_matters: This story shows that helping others doesn't always require a hospital or fancy tools—knowledge passed down in families can save lives, and everyone deserves respect for their skills.

background_read: Colombia is a country in South America with thick jungles and rivers that make travel hard, especially for people in small villages.
For hundreds of years, traditional midwives have helped mothers give birth in places where doctors and hospitals are not nearby.
Nohemí Manco (a Colombian midwife who has delivered about 1,200 babies) learned from watching her own mother.
Article_Structure: WHO: Nohemí Manco, a traditional midwife in Colombia, and other midwives like Yuvianis Florez.

WHAT: These traditional midwives, called 'parteras tradicionales,' deliver babies in remote jungle areas where hospitals are hard to reach. They face discrimination from doctors but want to work with modern medicine.
WHERE: In the jungles and rivers of Colombia, especially in faraway villages.
WHY: Because many pregnant women can't get to hospitals, and the midwives' tradition is at risk as many are over 60 and can't read; young people need to learn these lifesaving skills.

perspectives.description: They feel proud of their hundreds of years of knowledge and want doctors to treat them as equals. They believe combining old and new methods is best.
Some have been mean to midwives, maybe because they worry about safety without modern tools. They might not trust traditional birth methods.
They could learn midwifery skills to keep the tradition alive and help their communities, especially since many older midwives cannot read or write.
